input.question: If Voyager 1 is travelling at a speed of 38,000mph, and if just a small piece of space debris collides with it, wouldn't the probe break or have a major alteration in its course because of the immense speed?
input.ground_truth: The interstellar medium has a very low density, ~10^-4 ions/cm^3, this (roughly) equates to 1cm^3 of matter per cube of space, with a side length of 10,000 km. And most of that material will be individual ions. The chance of hitting anything out there is very remote.

Question: If Voyager 1 is travelling at a speed of 38,000mph, and if just a small piece of space debris collides with it, wouldn't the probe break or have a major alteration in its course because of the immense speed?

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine Voyager 1 is like a super fast toy car, and it’s zooming really, really fast—faster than any car you’ve ever seen! Now, imagine there’s a tiny pebble in space. If that tiny pebble hits Voyager 1, you might think, “Oh no! That will break it!”

But here’s the thing: space is *super* empty. There aren’t very many pebbles or things to bump into. Also, Voyager 1 is made of really strong materials, like a tough toy that can handle bumps.

Even though Voyager 1 is moving super fast, a tiny pebble doesn’t have much “oomph” to it because it’s so small and light. It’s kind of like when a tiny feather lands on your head while you’re running—it might tickle, but it doesn’t hurt you or knock you over.

So, if a tiny piece of space debris hits Voyager 1, it might make a little mark, but it probably won’t break the whole probe or make it fly off in a new direction. Scientists made Voyager 1 very strong, and space is so empty that these bumps are very, very rare.

But if a *really* big rock hit it, then yes, that could be a problem! But small pieces? Not so much.
